title: COPD: diagnosis, inhalers, pulmonary rehabilitation and home oxygen
blurb: Support an adult with stable COPD through diagnosis, inhaled treatment, rehabilitation, rescue packs and home oxygen decisions.
question: Mr Brennan, 64, has COPD and stops for breath after about 100 metres on the flat. He still smokes 15 cigarettes a day and asks whether he can have oxygen at home to help. What does NICE NG115 say?

teach.h: What COPD is and how it is confirmed
teach.body: Formally: COPD is airflow obstruction confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry with an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 in a person with typical symptoms (NG115). In plain English: the lungs cannot empty quickly, and inhalers do not fully reverse it. Suspect it in people over 35 with a risk factor, usually smoking, who have exertional breathlessness, chronic cough, regular sputum, frequent winter 'bronchitis' or wheeze.

bands.label: Breathless hurrying or on a slight hill
Slower than peers, or stops at own pace
Stops after about 100 m on the flat
Too breathless to leave the house

teach.caption: NG115 Table 1. MRC grade 3 and above usually means the person views themselves as functionally disabled: offer pulmonary rehabilitation.

steps.label: Foundations
steps.sub: stop smoking, vaccinations, rehab, inhaler technique

teach.caption: Asthmatic features: a secure previous diagnosis of asthma or atopy, higher blood eosinophils, FEV1 variation of at least 400 mL, or diurnal PEF variation of at least 20%.

teach.h: The nurse's part: smoking and technique
teach.body: Record pack-years (cigarettes per day ÷ 20 × years smoked) and, at every opportunity, advise and help the person to stop smoking. Check inhaler technique before anyone thinks about stepping treatment up: most people can learn adequate technique with training, and NICE advises minimising the number and types of inhalers. Discuss the risk of pneumonia with inhaled corticosteroids. Judge benefit by symptoms and daily activities, not lung function alone.

head: Question
NG115 answer
rows: Unable to walk, unstable angina, recent MI
teach.caption: NG115 1.2.82–1.2.85: programmes should be at convenient times and accessible places.

items: Agree an individualised exacerbation action plan with everyone at risk of exacerbations.

Offer a short course of oral corticosteroid and oral antibiotic to keep at home if they had an exacerbation in the last year, understand when and how to use them, and will tell the team and ask for replacements.
Steroid if breathlessness interferes with daily living; antibiotic if sputum changes colour and increases beyond normal variation.
At every review, check use; 3 or more courses in a year means investigate why.

root.label: Stable COPD, optimal treatment
root.sub: ABGs on 2 occasions at least 3 weeks apart

teach.caption: NG115 1.2.58–1.2.64. Use for at least 15 hours a day; concentrator at home; not for isolated nocturnal hypoxaemia; review at least yearly with oximetry.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr Brennan in a GP respiratory clinic
teach.body: Mr Brennan stops after about 100 m on the flat (MRC 4), so practice nurse Adaeze refers him to pulmonary rehabilitation and watches his inhaler technique, correcting it. He asks for home oxygen. She explains LTOT is assessed with blood gases when stable, and that NICE does not offer it to people who continue to smoke because of the fire and burns risk. She offers stop-smoking treatment and a referral to specialist services, and agrees an exacerbation action plan with him.

teach.text: Home oxygen is not a treatment for breathlessness. LTOT is decided by arterial PaO2 when stable, not by how breathless someone feels, and it is not offered to people who keep smoking. Ambulatory oxygen is not offered for breathlessness when there is mild or no hypoxaemia at rest.

items: Diagnosis: symptoms plus post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7; suspect in over-35s with a risk factor.
Stop smoking support at every opportunity; check inhaler technique before stepping up.
SABA/SAMA first, then LAMA+LABA (or LABA+ICS if asthmatic features), triple therapy after review.
Pulmonary rehab for MRC 3+, including after an admission; rescue pack with a written action plan.
LTOT: PaO2 below 7.3 kPa (or 7.3–8 with complications), not if smoking, 15 h/day, yearly review.

summary: You can now explain how COPD is confirmed and graded, how inhaled treatment is built up and where nurses add most value (smoking cessation and inhaler technique). You can also apply NICE criteria for pulmonary rehabilitation, rescue packs and long-term oxygen therapy.

A.q: Which spirometry result confirms airflow obstruction in suspected COPD?
A.why: NG115: airflow obstruction is defined as a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7.

whyNot.1: FEV1 % predicted grades severity; it is the ratio that confirms obstruction.
whyNot.2: FVC is a volume, not a ratio, and is not the diagnostic criterion.
whyNot.3: Peak flow variability of 20% or more suggests asthmatic features, not COPD.

A.q: A man with COPD says he walks slower than people his age because of breathlessness. Which MRC grade is this?
A.why: MRC grade 3: walks slower than contemporaries on level ground because of breathlessness, or has to stop for breath when walking at own pace.

whyNot.0: Grade 1 is breathlessness on strenuous exercise.
whyNot.1: Grade 2 is breathlessness when hurrying or walking up a slight hill.
whyNot.2: Grade 4 is stopping for breath after about 100 m on the flat.

A.q: A woman with COPD (no asthmatic features) remains breathless despite a SABA, optimised non-drug care and vaccinations. What does NG115 recommend next?
A.why: NG115 1.2.10: offer LAMA+LABA to people with confirmed COPD without asthmatic features who remain breathless or have exacerbations despite these measures.

whyNot.0: Maintenance oral corticosteroids are not a routine step.
whyNot.1: LABA+ICS is considered when there are asthmatic features.
whyNot.3: Theophylline is not the next step in NG115.

B.q: Which patient with COPD is most suitable for referral to pulmonary rehabilitation?
options: A man with unstable angina at rest
A woman who cannot walk unaided or with aids
A man who had an MI two weeks ago
B.why: NG115 1.2.83: offer pulmonary rehabilitation to people who view themselves as functionally disabled, usually MRC grade 3 and above.

whyNot.0: Unstable angina makes pulmonary rehabilitation unsuitable.
whyNot.1: People who are unable to walk are not suitable.
whyNot.2: A recent myocardial infarction makes it unsuitable.

B.q: A man with COPD keeps a rescue pack at home. At review he has used 3 courses of prednisolone and antibiotics this year. What should happen?
options: Find out why he needed them
Give a larger pack so it lasts longer
Stop the rescue pack from now onwards
Add a fourth course to cover winter
B.why: NG115 1.2.130: for people who have used 3 or more courses of oral corticosteroids and/or antibiotics in the last year, investigate the possible reasons.

whyNot.1: More supply does not address why exacerbations are frequent.
whyNot.2: Stopping the pack removes a useful part of his action plan.
whyNot.3: Extra courses without review miss the cause.

B.q: A woman being assessed for long-term oxygen therapy asks how long she would need to use it each day. What is the correct advice?
B.why: NG115 1.2.63: people on LTOT should breathe supplemental oxygen for a minimum of 15 hours per day.

whyNot.0: 8 hours is below the NICE minimum.
whyNot.1: 12 hours is below the NICE minimum.
whyNot.3: NICE sets the minimum at 15 hours, not 20.

C.q: Mr Patel, 69, has stable COPD. Two ABGs 4 weeks apart show PaO2 7.6 kPa. He has peripheral oedema and does not smoke. What does NICE advise?
options: LTOT is not indicated above 7.3 kPa
Ambulatory oxygen in place of LTOT
C.why: NG115 1.2.59: consider LTOT if PaO2 is above 7.3 and below 8 kPa when stable with secondary polycythaemia, peripheral oedema or pulmonary hypertension, in people who do not smoke.

whyNot.0: Between 7.3 and 8 kPa, LTOT is considered when complications such as oedema are present.
whyNot.2: Ambulatory oxygen is for exercise desaturation after specialist assessment, not a substitute.
whyNot.3: NICE does not offer LTOT for isolated nocturnal hypoxaemia.

C.q: Mrs Ford, 72, with COPD, asks for home oxygen for breathlessness on exertion. Her resting SpO2 is 95% on air. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Arrange LTOT as she is breathless
Arrange a concentrator for night use
Arrange ambulatory oxygen to help her walking
Explain oxygen will not help at that level
C.why: NG115 1.2.68: do not offer ambulatory oxygen to manage breathlessness in people with mild or no hypoxaemia at rest. Oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness; rehabilitation and optimised treatment help more.

whyNot.0: LTOT is based on PaO2 when stable, not breathlessness.
whyNot.1: A concentrator supplies LTOT, which she does not meet criteria for.
whyNot.2: Ambulatory oxygen is not offered for breathlessness without significant hypoxaemia.

C.q: A man with COPD on LAMA+LABA is still breathless. On review his inhaler technique is poor and he smokes. What should the nurse address first?
options: Request triple therapy from the GP
Switch to a nebuliser at home
Add an oral antibiotic for prevention
C.why: NG115: check technique and optimise non-pharmacological care, including stop-smoking treatment, before escalating. Triple therapy requires a clinical review confirming these are optimised (1.2.13).

whyNot.0: Stepping up before correcting technique and smoking does not follow NG115.
whyNot.2: A nebuliser is not the answer to poor handheld technique.
whyNot.3: Prophylactic antibiotics are reserved for selected patients after other measures.

reteach.title: Four pillars of stable COPD care
reteach.question: If you had to hold up one person's COPD care with four pillars, what would they be?

blocks.body: Breathe: the right inhalers, used properly, starting with short-acting and stepping to LAMA+LABA. Move: pulmonary rehabilitation for anyone limited by breathlessness (MRC 3+). Plan: a written action plan with a rescue pack, reviewed every visit. Oxygenate: only if blood gases show chronic hypoxaemia, only without smoking, for at least 15 hours a day. Under all four sits stopping smoking.

blocks.text: LTOT is never a reward for being breathless: it depends on PaO2 below 7.3 kPa (or 7.3–8 kPa with polycythaemia, oedema or pulmonary hypertension) and not smoking.

explain.body: Symptoms plus post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7. Suspect in over-35s with a risk factor. Record pack-years: cigarettes per day ÷ 20 × years.

test.q: A woman has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 30 years. How many pack-years is this?
test.why: Pack-years = cigarettes per day ÷ 20 × years smoked = 20 ÷ 20 × 30 = 30.

whyNot.0: 20 is the number of cigarettes per day, not pack-years.

explain.body: Short-acting bronchodilator first. Then LAMA+LABA if no asthmatic features, or consider LABA+ICS if asthmatic features. Discuss pneumonia risk with ICS.

test.q: Which side effect should be discussed with a person with COPD starting an inhaled corticosteroid?
test.why: NG115 1.2.8: be prepared to discuss the risk of side effects, including pneumonia, in people taking ICS for COPD.

whyNot.1: Hypoglycaemia is not a recognised ICS risk.
whyNot.2: Gout is not an ICS risk highlighted by NICE.
whyNot.3: Tinnitus is not an ICS risk highlighted by NICE.

explain.body: Pulmonary rehabilitation for MRC 3+ (not if unable to walk, unstable angina, recent MI). Rescue pack of oral steroid and antibiotic with an individual action plan for those at risk of exacerbations.

test.q: According to a COPD action plan, when should a person add the antibiotic from their rescue pack?
options: When they feel more tired than usual
When they need their SABA once in a single day
When sputum is darker and greater in amount
When they develop a dry cough at night
test.why: NG115 1.2.132: add oral antibiotics if sputum changes colour and increases in volume or thickness beyond normal day-to-day variation.

whyNot.0: Tiredness is not the antibiotic trigger.
whyNot.1: Occasional reliever use does not trigger antibiotics.
whyNot.3: A dry cough is not the trigger described.

explain.body: ABGs twice, at least 3 weeks apart, when stable. Consider LTOT if PaO2 below 7.3 kPa, or 7.3–8 kPa with polycythaemia, oedema or pulmonary hypertension. Not if still smoking. At least 15 hours a day; yearly review.

test.q: How should a person with stable COPD be assessed for long-term oxygen therapy?
test.why: NG115 1.2.58: measure arterial blood gases on 2 occasions at least 3 weeks apart in people with a confident diagnosis, on optimal treatment and stable.

whyNot.0: Oximetry identifies who to assess but does not decide LTOT.
whyNot.1: A walk test is used for ambulatory oxygen assessment, not LTOT.
whyNot.3: LTOT is not offered for isolated nocturnal hypoxaemia.
